summary: Offers advice for people who organize informal side meetings, called Bar BOFs, at IETF meetings to develop new work. Such meetings are not on the official agenda and have no official status. It is informational.

eli5.summary: Before starting a new club at school, friends sometimes meet at lunch to plan. This memo gives tips for making those unofficial meetings work well.

questions: how to run a bar bof
how to run an ietf side meeting
why stop calling them bar bofs
subtitle: Advice for running unofficial IETF side meetings that actually help develop new work.

tldr.problem: Unofficial "bar BOF" get-togethers at IETF meetings had become hard to tell from official BOFs and working group meetings, which hurts their goal of brainstorming new work.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC recommends calling them "side meetings" and advises on whom to invite, where, how and when to meet, favoring small, informal gatherings with food and drink.
tldr.outcome: It is advice only, published as an Informational document, and stresses that side meetings have no official status.

today: RFC 6771 is an Informational document that has not been obsoleted or updated. It gives advice rather than rules, and side meetings remain unofficial.

sections.title: Side Meetings, Not Bar BOFs
sections.content:
Besides official sessions, an IETF meeting hosts many unofficial ones. Some are organized to start new IETF work. These have commonly been called bar BOFs, after the official "birds of a feather" (BOF) session. Lately they have become hard to distinguish from official BOFs or even working group meetings, with classroom seating, lengthy slides, microphone lines and formal consensus calls, and, as the RFC notes, a distinct lack of drinks.

The RFC recommends dropping the term "bar BOF" in favor of side meeting. Some participants even believed a bar BOF was a required step before an official BOF, which is false. It also reminds organizers that conference calls, email, wikis and group chats can develop ideas and are easier to schedule.
sections.eli5: Calling an unofficial chat a BOF makes people think it is the real thing. A new name, side meeting, makes clear it is just friends talking.

sections.title: How to Invite
sections.content:
A side meeting should include the people needed to reach its purpose and no more, since smaller meetings are usually more successful. Announcing publicly can draw large crowds, including "tourists" who turn a discussion into a tutorial. If you do announce, the RFC suggests asking would-be attendees to explain how they will contribute.

Inviting IESG or IAB members is not necessary and may not be advisable while an idea is still forming, and their attendance or absence is not a sign of support or disapproval. Smaller groups also limit scope creep. Attendance numbers have no influence on whether new work is approved, which depends on technical merit and community energy. An "ad hoc session" of a working group is no more official, and working group consensus can only be established in official sessions or on the mailing list (RFC 2418).
sections.eli5: Invite only the friends who will help with the plan. A giant crowd just makes things messy, and who shows up does not decide whether the club gets approved.

sections.title: Where and How to Meet
sections.content:
Side meetings are traditionally held in bars or restaurants. Many have shifted into IETF meeting rooms, partly because noisy venues are hard for some participants and partly because booking a room needs Area Director approval. That approval is not an expression of support for the topic.

Meeting rooms are poor for brainstorming: classroom seating and microphones suit presentations, not discussion, and booking only outside working hours pushes meetings into meal times. The RFC says food, drink and a relaxed atmosphere are an essential part of a successful side meeting. It also warns against imitating official meetings with agendas, chairs, blue sheets and hums, which is unproductive and confusing. In one case, participants believed they were attending an actual working group meeting.
sections.eli5: Plan the club over a snack around a table, not in a big hall with a microphone. Do not pretend to be a real meeting, since people may get confused.

sections.title: When to Meet and Where to Gather Input
sections.content:
Side meetings often follow IETF evening plenaries, which can end early or very late. The RFC recommends scheduling them relative to the end, such as "X minutes after the end of the plenary", rather than at a fixed time.

Citing RFC 5434, it adds that understanding a problem fully means hearing from other communities too, such as operators and researchers. Organizers should consider venues like operator fora (RIPE, NANOG, etc.) and research conferences.
sections.eli5: If the big talk ends early or late, start your chat a set time after it ends, so nobody waits or has to leave early.

sections.title: Conclusions and Security
sections.content:
Organizers are encouraged to rekindle the original spirit of side meetings: outside IETF meeting rooms, with food and drink, for smaller groups, and without mimicking official sessions. All side meetings during an IETF week are purely informal and have no official status whatsoever.

The Security Considerations section is a joke of sorts. People have been known to forget laptops after side meetings in real bars, so organizers should remind any attending security Area Directors to take their belongings when the bar closes or the meeting ends, whichever happens first.
sections.eli5: Keep it small and friendly, and remember to take your backpack home when you leave.
